observation: The re-review did not stop at 'the fix is present'. It diffed the re-homed assertions byte-for-byte against git history, then asked whether the restored test can fail: commenting out the guarantee's early return left the test GREEN, because a unique index and a raced-select fallback reproduce the observable behaviour; corrupting the identity at the insert produced a real RED. It reasoned through whether that redundancy means the protection is weaker than it looks, concluded the two mechanisms coincide for every producible input, and then declined to strengthen the test past the protected baseline because that would be new scope.

observation: The planned fix for the last remaining violation turned out to be illegal, and the builder reverted rather than forced it. The architecture had the owning service re-export the generated table schema; no-laundered-re-exports forbids republishing a table symbol across a package boundary 'not even by its owner, because that is precisely how a consumer' obtains it, and the rule catches the value-alias spelling too. The replacement — core-api hand-writing the wire shape — then exposed that the table-derived schema had been wrong all along: at_risk is an integer column the route normalizes to a boolean before responding, so fed the row its own endpoint emits, the schema rejected it.
evidence: progress.json buildPlan.blockedItem (whyPlanFailed, latentBugFound); scripts/rules/no-laundered-re-exports.ts:29-30,:224; commit 4ec0c14b message

observation: The wrong schema survived because the only test that ever parsed a live response inserted no bet — it had only ever validated four empty arrays. A schema contradicting its own endpoint sat in the tree passing every gate. The fix inserts a real bet and asserts the group is non-empty before parsing, so the parse can no longer succeed against emptiness.

observation: This work package's own new test was flaky at roughly three runs in ten. The assertions read rows back through a query ordered by a millisecond-resolution timestamp; the fixtures write several rows for one task inside the same millisecond, so the sort was not a total order and fell through to its ordinal tiebreak. The fix had to preserve the distinction the case exists to make — ordering-by-ordinal alone would have gone green under a max(ordinal)+1 implementation — so it addressed rows by identity instead, and the reviewer re-proved the distinction by mutation.
evidence: commit ee7ee420 message; review-2.md:149-152 (max(ordinal)+1 substitution → 'expected 10 to be 2')

observation: The recurring shape across this run is a claim asserted from reading rather than from running, and it recurred at every phase and in every role. Instances: the acceptance criterion whose proof was a severity-blind harness; the test cited as asserting an ordinal it never names; the 'zero callers — verified' helper with eleven callers; the 'three of its four tests' file that held five; the 'exact list' of 20 test files that was 21; the post-commit sweep the plan claims returns nothing while its own sibling section requires three lines; a sibling work package inferred unstarted from a missing file; an orchestrator brief asserting a live branch was dead; a critique blessing a re-export the lint forbids outright. Every one was caught by someone who ran something — a lint, an rg, a git show, a probe. None was caught by a second careful reading.

observation: The second recurring shape is a proof that existed but could not go red. Instances: the attack harness that hardcodes severity and passed before the change it was cited for; the migration table-list assertions using arrayContaining, where removing a name is a no-op in both directions; the response-schema test that only ever validated four empty arrays; the handoff test that reaches the insert but cannot see a wrong ordinal; the ESLint block that would have kept reporting clean against a deleted file; the governance check that reads the live table list from source and would never notice a database keeping a dropped table; and the deleted idempotency test, where verify was green because the assertion was gone. Two of these — the empty-array parse and the deleted test — were hiding a real defect at the moment they were found.

observation: Phases run: refine (+1 critique round, BLOCKED on 3, closed in one revision), architecture (2 critique rounds — the main pass BLOCKED on 1, the Ruling-4 amendment pass BLOCKED on 4, both closed), founder concept gate (5 binding rulings, one a deliberate scope change absorbing an unstarted work package's charter), build (one builder, sequential, 8 planned commits), implementation review (2 rounds — NOT DONE then DONE), 1 rebase. No 4th planning critique: the decision to proceed on the ground that remaining risk was execution is recorded in progress state. 18 commits over 94 files: 7 delivery commits, 1 revert-and-replace after the planned fix proved illegal, 4 review- and defect-driven fix commits (1 blocking re-home, 3 non-blocking), 1 flake fix, 5 attestation mints, 1 artifact commit. Rework and process overhead: 3 planning revision rounds, 1 code fix cycle, 1 reverted plan step, 1 flaky test introduced and fixed, 5 attestations, and 3 plan/repo contradictions resolved at build. No new package was created — the plan said one had to be, and the founder ruling removed it. Net: 191 → 90 production governance violations, 100 → 0 table violations, 0 development throughout, ten table rule keys promoted from warn to error, verify green.
